subject: EDGE.md -- the whole thread written up, and the one finding that matters most
body:
EDGE.md is in files/from-agent -- the whole thread written up properly. Here is the shape of it.

THE WORD WAS DOING THREE JOBS. Directional edge: a high score means price goes that way. Selective edge: in some moments it is right and we can tell which in advance. Structural edge: direction is a coin flip but the payoff geometry is not. Nearly every disagreement we have had was two of those being compared as if they were one thing.

THE ARITHMETIC. Expectancy is p times the average win, minus one-minus-p times the average loss. Three levers, not four -- winning more often and losing less often are the same number. And the three cannot be set independently: widen the target and the win rate falls, tighten the stop and it falls faster. You slide along one curve.

WHAT WE MEASURED. Direction: absent, at every horizon, after correcting for how many tests we have run and for the fact that overlapping bars are not independent observations. That null is now as solid as it can honestly be made. Selectivity: not present in the blended score -- but that measures downstream of the blend, and if two indicators lean opposite ways in the same moment the blend is flat there AND flat overall. The cancelling happens before the score exists. That is one calibration run from being answered, and the instrument is built and proven on a planted case.

Geometry: the finding I trust most in the whole document. The median adverse excursion is 1.55 ATR and our stop sits at 1.50. The stop is inside the noise -- it gets hit by 56% of bars regardless of direction, while our target is reached by 30%. Almost twice as often. And the bracket we run scores minus 0.05R, just under break-even, ranking 63rd of the 80 I tried.

That is also the precise answer to the video. Losing as little as possible is the trap here, not the cure -- our stop is already tight enough to be triggered by noise more often than the target is reached by signal.

FOUR TIMES TODAY MY OWN ANALYSIS WAS WRONG IN OUR FAVOUR AND I CAUGHT IT. Wide stops looked profitable until I noticed a 3.0 stop is only ever reached by 3.4% of bars -- it was not a wide stop, it was no stop, and no stop always wins over a window short enough to hide the tail. All four are written up, because the pattern of the day was that the instruments were wrong far more often than the system.

FIVE THINGS ARE BUILT AND CONNECTED TO NOTHING. The living-edge cell layer computes a posterior edge and a position size on every regime and prints them to a log line -- its own comment says it changes nothing. The tradeable gate, the cell-informed exits, the driver fingerprint: zero callers. And meta-labelling -- the published method for exactly what you described, keep the signal and train a second model to decide when to act on it -- is sitting in our own toolkit, self-tested, used nowhere.

THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST. Calibration does not optimise your equation. It maximises win rate times profit factor, with expectancy allowed in only as a bonus capped at thirty percent. It is grinding on the one lever we have proven does not move. Worse, it picks the weights first and the exit brackets afterwards, in separate phases -- so the three coupled numbers are never chosen together. And it arms on a pooled win rate, which averages the good moments in with everything else, which is exactly the operation that destroys a selective edge.

The right objective is already in our code. The quarantine drops a regime on expectancy below 0.10R -- per regime, expectancy-based, exactly right. We use it at the end to reject rather than at the front to select.

You are right that we should train hard at maximising that equation. The reason we have not is that the search is pointed at a different quantity, in an order that prevents it, behind a gate that undoes it.
